transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-24
Time: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Oliver Hayes (Stonehaven Head of ML), Priya Nair (Director of Infra), Marcus Lee (Quant Eng)

Summary:
High-level cost economics discovery focused on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options. Customer shared workload characteristics (average tokens, tail latencies, qps), constraint: monthly budget ceiling, strong security/compliance needs. Discussed batching and KV/prefix caching levers, quantization impacts, and suggested pilot/benchmark next steps.

Topics:
- Current stack & constraints
- Per-token pricing and unit economics
- Batching/caching strategies and latency tradeoffs
- Dedicated capacity vs hosted pricing/commits
- Security (KMS/SOC2, VPC) concerns
- Pilot/bench plan and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, i'll kick us off and then ethan will do the technical bits, uh could we do quick intros?
[00:08] Oliver: sure, i'm oliver, head of ml at stonehaven, we run models for quant signals and research summarization, mostly in-house infra right now.
[00:15] Priya: priya - infra, i look after deploy and security.
[00:18] Marcus: marcus, quant engineer, building the model scoring pipeline.
[00:21] Ethan: ethan, solutions engineer - i focus on latency/cost optimizations and benching.
[00:26] Maya: awesome. quick context: you asked to talk through cost/unit economics for host vs dedicated vs private — we want to understand your qps, avg tokens, and budget to recommend a path. oliver, do you wanna share numbers?
[00:36] Oliver: yeah so basic shape - production is about 1.2k qpm at peak, avg tokens per request around 420 tokens, tails up to 2k for some research prompts. monthly active requests ~ 5.2M. budget is roughly $45k/month for inference to start, we can stretch for a pilot if results look good.
[00:52] Priya: and security: we need SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS integration for keys, and data residency in us-east for now.
[00:58] Maya: good, that helps. rough mental model: hosted is easiest to start (no infra), dedicated gives predictable throughput via reserved capacity and lower unit cost at scale, and private gives you full control + compliance but has operational overhead.
[01:10] Ethan: on the cost side — there are a few levers: per-token base price, batching (we can batch to reduce per-token GPU cost but it increases latency), KV/prefix caching for repeated prefixes which cuts tokens processed, and model quantization options (int8/4bit) that change throughput and memory.
[01:24] Marcus: couple questions — how much does batching actually move the needle? our median latency target 200ms p95 is strict for trader-facing features.
[01:32] Ethan: great question. for your workload distribution, if requests are independent and short, batching gives big wins; but since you have long tokens and tails, the effective batching window might be limited. example: continuous batching can batch small windows (10-20ms) to get modest gains; larger batching (50-200ms) gives more cost reduction but pushes latency beyond p95 target. caching helps more for repeated prefixes — like prompt templates for summarization - you can get 30-60% token reduction for those flows.
[01:53] Oliver: hmm we do have a lot of repeated prefixes for doc summaries, but research scoring prompts are quite unique. so maybe hybrid.
[01:59] Maya: exactly — we typically recommend a mixed strategy: hosted to validate, then move to dedicated reserved capacity for steady scoring loads and keep hosted or burst for spikes. dedicated price per token is lower with month/annual commit.
[02:12] Priya: on private — we can't do on-prem right away, but vpc/private control plane with KMS would be required for production. is that available?
[02:19] Ethan: yes our Private option supports customer-managed networking, KMS/HSM integration, and we provide audit logs. there is more setup time and a platform fee. tradeoff is full data control and predictable costs if you own infra.
[02:28] Marcus: can you walk through an example math for per-token cost comparing hosted vs dedicated?
[02:32] Maya: sure - i'll keep it illustrative. on hosted our list price for a 13B-ish model is X per 1k tokens (note: pricing slightly obfuscated in transcript), but for simplicity say hosted is $0.03 per 1k tokens at baseline. with your 5.2M calls * 420 tokens avg that's ~2.18B tokens/month, so hosted would be around $65k/mo before discounts.
[02:55] Ethan: with batching and caching you could shrink the effective processed tokens by 20-35% depending on workload; so if you implement prefix caching for summaries and small batching for scoring, maybe you get to ~1.6B effective tokens which drops cost proportionally.
[03:08] Maya: dedicated reserved capacity might price at, say, $Y per token roughly 20-40% lower than hosted at commit levels - plus you get predictable throughput and burst capacity options. so with dedicated you might land near your $45k budget if caching/batching are applied and you do a 6-12 month commit.
[03:23] Priya: okay that sounds promising. what's the ramp/commit needed for dedicated? minimum GPUs or commit?
[03:28] Ethan: typically we size dedicated pools by required concurrency and model memory needs. for your 1.2k qpm peak and 420 avg token, we'd propose a pool with N A100-ish equivalents (we'll run bench to size exactly). commit tiers start at a few hundred hours/month per GPU equivalent - i'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[03:41] Oliver: if we do dedicated, do we still pay for egress or network costs separately?
[03:45] Maya: egress can be separate depending on cloud region, but for many customers it's small relative to token costs. we'll call out any additional infra or region fees in the proposal.
[03:53] Marcus: back to caching — how does Redwood's KV cache work? does it require model changes or is it runtime-level?
[03:59] Ethan: it's runtime-level — we support prefix caching and KV cache for autoregressive traces (like LLM generation). it stores token-level KV cache so repeated prefixes skip compute. it works without model surgery but is most effective when prompts have shared prefixes across many requests. there are TTLs and eviction policies; we can configure by route.
[04:15] Oliver: do you have examples where KV cache cut costs materially?
[04:18] Ethan: yes — one customer saw 40% token savings on their doc-summary flows; another with heavy repeated prompts saw 60% reduction for that route. overall company-level savings depends on how much of traffic is cacheable.
[04:27] Priya: security again — SOC2 and SAML? we need SOC2 Type II and SAML-based SSO, also enterprise audit logs for token-level tracing (not content, but metadata).
[04:36] Maya: we are SOC2, we can provide the report; SSO/SAML is supported, RBAC and audit logs available. for private deployments we can route logs to your SIEM, and KMS for key control.
[04:46] Oliver: what's the timeline to run a bench and get an exact cost?
[04:49] Ethan: we can spin up a bench harness quick — require sample prompts and a token distribution, then we'll run a 48-hour throughput test that measures latency, throughput, and effective token consumption with different batching/caching configs. we typically get results within a week of data.
[05:01] Maya: action item: ethan will propose the bench plan and needed artifacts, maya will send the cost spreadsheet.
[05:06] Marcus: a few nitty gritty: do you support quantized models (4-bit) on hosted or only on dedicated? and what's impact on quality?
[05:13] Ethan: we support quantized variants on both hosted and dedicated where the model supports it; dedicated gives more flexibility for custom kernels and more aggressive quantization. quality impact varies by model; usually 4-bit int8/4bit has minor delta on many tasks, but we recommend running eval sets — which we can do as part of the bench.
[05:29] Oliver: curious about fallbacks — if dedicated capacity is saturated, can requests spill to hosted?
[05:33] Ethan: yes, smart routing supports fallbacks by policy — you can route spikes to hosted or a cheaper region. you can set SLO rules to prefer latency or cost.
[05:40] Priya: on logging and data handling — will logs contain request text in hosted? we need to avoid customer PII in logs.
[05:46] Maya: by default we retain minimal metadata, and content retention policies can be configured; for regulated flows we'd recommend private or dedicated with strict retention and optional content redaction. we'll share our data handling doc.
[05:56] Marcus: any limitations on model catalog? we use some open models and a custom finetuned variant.
[06:00] Ethan: we support a variety of open models and bring-your-own-model in Private and Dedicated (you can upload or point to your model artifacts). hosted supports curated open models and Redwood-verified performance profiles; for custom finetuned models dedicated/private is the path.
[06:11] Oliver: cost example: if we do a pilot with dedicated for scoring only (steady 700 qpm) and keep research on hosted, does that simplify sizing?
[06:19] Ethan: absolutely — segmenting routes lets you optimize: dedicate capacity for steady scoring (commit to get lower unit costs) and leave bursty or long-tail research on hosted. caching and batching configs can differ by route.
[06:30] Maya: ok we're approaching time. quick recap and next steps — maya sends spreadsheet with hosted vs dedicated vs private illustrative pricing; ethan sends bench plan and prompt list; stonehaven shares token distribution and any compliance paperwork. agree to reconvene after bench.
[06:43] Oliver: yes that works. thanks all.
[06:45] Maya: thanks, i'll follow up with calendar and docs. bye.
